values.title: Four programs, one harvest
values.intro: The gardens feed the market, the market asks for nothing in return, and the clubs and workshops raise the next crew of growers.

image.alt: Neighbours watering raised beds at the Orchard Terrace garden in the evening

items.label: 01 · Community gardens
items.title: A plot of your own, or a row of ours
items.text: Larkin Lot, Orchard Terrace and the Whitcomb schoolyard hold 142 plots. Household plots are free and come with water, tools and seedlings. Prefer company? Join a work party and grow for the market.

image.alt: Tables of squash, onions, bread and eggs at the free market in Commons House

items.label: 02 · Wednesday free market
items.title: Shop like it is a farm stand
items.text: Every Wednesday from 3 to 6:30 pm we set out what the gardens, local farms and two bakeries brought in. Take what your household will eat. We never ask for ID, income or an address.

image.alt: Children chopping vegetables with a Sprouts club leader in a school kitchen

items.label: 03 · Sprouts youth clubs
items.title: Lunch they planted themselves
items.text: Sprouts clubs meet after school in six elementary schools. Kids from kindergarten to fifth grade sow, weed, harvest and cook, and take a bag of vegetables home each week.

image.alt: Shovels, rakes and a wheelbarrow hanging in the tool library shed

items.label: 04 · Tool library and workshops
items.title: Borrow a broadfork, learn to prune
items.text: Members borrow from 260 tools for free. Saturday workshops cover composting, seed saving, canning and fruit tree care, taught by neighbours who have done it for decades.

values.title: Before you come
values.intro: The questions we hear most at the garden gate and the market door.

items.question: Is the market really free?
items.detail: Take what your household will eat. There is no charge and no limit on visits.

items.question: Do I need ID or proof of income?
items.detail: We ask your first name and household size, and only so we can plan the harvest.

items.question: Do I need gardening experience?
items.detail: Every work party starts with a ten-minute walk-through for newcomers.

items.question: Can children come along?
items.detail: All ages are welcome with an adult. We keep child-size tools in the shed.

items.question: Are plots open right now?
items.detail: Plots are assigned each March. The 2027 list opens on January 5.

items.question: Can I drop off garden surplus?
items.detail: Bring it to Commons House any Wednesday morning before noon.

values.title: Food is a neighbourhood project
values.text: Sparrow Hill Commons began in 2011, when eleven neighbours cleared a vacant lot on Larkin Avenue and built 24 garden beds from salvaged cedar. Fifteen years on, these are still the rules we work by.

principles.title: Nobody proves they are hungry
principles.text: We do not ask for ID, income or a reason. Dignity comes first.

principles.title: Grown here, by us
principles.text: Most of what we share is planted within a mile of the market door.

principles.title: Neighbours lead
principles.text: Seven of our eleven board members grow or shop with us.

principles.title: Share the know-how too
principles.text: Every harvest comes with a recipe, a workshop or a seed packet.

values.title: From one vacant lot to three gardens
values.intro: We have grown slowly and on purpose, adding a garden or a program only when neighbours asked for it and offered to help run it.

milestones.title: The Larkin Lot is cleared
milestones.text: Eleven neighbours haul out two dumpsters of rubble and build 24 beds. The first harvest is mostly zucchini.

milestones.title: A card table becomes the free market
milestones.text: Gardeners start leaving surplus on a table by the gate each Wednesday. By autumn, 60 households stop by every week.

milestones.title: Orchard Terrace is planted
milestones.text: The city leases us a hillside. Volunteers terrace it and plant 48 apple, pear and plum trees.

milestones.title: Sprouts starts at Whitcomb Elementary
milestones.text: One teacher, one raised bed and 14 kids. Six schools have joined since.

milestones.title: We move into Commons House
milestones.text: A former corner grocery becomes our market hall, kitchen, seed room and tool library.

milestones.title: A winter greenhouse breaks ground
milestones.text: With a heated greenhouse on Orchard Terrace, the market will have fresh greens in January for the first time.

values.title: A letter we read aloud at the harvest fair
values.letter:
When my hours were cut last winter I started coming to the market on Wednesdays. Nobody asked me a single question. Ngoc Anh just handed me a bag and told me the squash was good that week.
In April I took a plot at Orchard Terrace. This month I carried my own tomatoes to the market table for somebody else to take home. I wanted the people who pay for all of this to know what it turned into.
values.name: Darlene Whitaker

values.title: Before you give
values.intro: Four things donors ask Priya most often.

items.question: Is my gift tax-deductible?
items.answer: Yes. Sparrow Hill Commons is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, and gifts are deductible in the United States as far as the law allows. You get a receipt by email right away and a yearly summary each January.

items.question: Can I change or cancel a monthly gift?
items.answer: Any time. Reply to any receipt or call Priya on +1 509 555 0164 and it is done the same day, with no forms to fill in.

items.question: Can I give something other than money?
items.answer: Gladly. We take garden surplus on Wednesday mornings, clean tools for the library, and stock or donor-advised fund gifts. Many employers also match gifts, so it is worth asking yours.

items.question: Can I leave a gift in my will?
items.answer: Yes, and several neighbours have. Write to giving@sparrowhill.example and Priya will send the wording your lawyer needs.
